newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian premier quits, new cabinet to be formed.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian premier quits, new cabinet to be formed.

text.p: Bulgarian Prime Minister Zhan Videnov on Saturday presented the resignation of his cabinet at a congress of his Bulgarian Socialist Party and said he would not seek re-election as premier or party leader.

"As of this morning, parliament will have the resignation of the government. This will enable the Democratic Left to present for support in parliament the government Bulgaria needs today," he told the opening session of the congress.
Videnov said he felt he lacked the necessary support from party colleagues and from society as a whole to continue as premier, and the congress would appoint a new cabinet headed by someone else.
"I declare my firm intention not to run for a leading post in the party or the government," said Videnov, who became prime minister when the Socialists won parliamentary elections in December 1994.
Leading members of the Bulgarian Communist Party renamed themselves Socialists after the collapse of one-party rule in 1989. They also refer to themselves as the Democratic Left.

Videnov said he believed his resignation would help satisfy opposition demands that tough economic reforms be introduced by political consensus, while sparing the country the need for parliamentary elections.

Criticism of Videnov's handling of severe economic crisis increased following the Socialist party's decisive defeat in last month's presidential elections, but in the short term, naming a new government may delay planned reforms.
Bulgaria is preparing to introduce a currency board fixed exchange rate regime to halt the fall of the national currency, and has not yet finalised the 1997 budget.
The lev has collapsed from 70 to the dollar at the beginning of the year to 485 now.

IMF technical experts left on Friday after 10 days in Sofia helping the government to prepare the legal adjustments for restructuring the central bank into a currency board and to draft the 1997 budget.

IMF mission head Anne McGuirk said she hoped to be back in the New Year. "A lot depends on how long it takes to resolve the political situation and then we can come back and do the actual negotiation," she told reporters at the airport on Friday.
